extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, media scholars and watchdogs interested in photojournalism ethics and media controversies
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating the authenticity, ethicality, and editorial handling of news photographs (particularly wartime images) with attention to manipulation, staging, captioning, and organizational responses. The page documents examples from the 2006 Lebanon War that illustrate these concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digitally manipulated photographs
rubrics_metrics.description: “Digitally manipulated photographs” (e.g., Adnan Hajj) — photographs altered with software to misrepresent scenes of death and destruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples on page: adding and darkening smoke spirals in a Beirut photo; cloning a flare to make one defensive flare appear as multiple missiles; added plume of smoke and duplicated buildings. Detection by bloggers and analysts (e.g., evidence of cloning/Adobe Photoshop clone stamp). Antipattern: publishing doctored images without verification. Remedial actions shown: removal of images and termination of cooperation with the photographer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial policy prohibiting alteration
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations should adhere to editorial policies that forbid altering pictures — e.g., Reuters statement that “it is strictly against company editorial policy to alter pictures.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizational responses illustrated: immediate removal of altered images, issuing apologies, publishing corrected versions, stopping cooperation with implicated freelancers, and conducting internal investigations (which in Reuters' case led to firing a top photo editor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Photo editing software used improperly
rubrics_metrics.description: “Photo editing software was improperly used on this image.” — improper use of editing tools (clone stamp, etc.) that changes documentary content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signs of improper use: repeating patterns, duplicated elements (smoke plumes, buildings), impossible lighting/reflection artifacts. Guidance: examine originals, technical forensic checks; blogs and photo-forensics can detect such markers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct identification of objects/actions (avoid misidentification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid misidentifying objects or actions in photos (example: defensive flares misidentified as air-to-ground missiles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare with originals and context before captioning; consult technical/military experts when identifying weaponry or tactics; bloggers uncovered misidentification by comparing originals and noting doctored duplication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid staging or orchestration for cameras
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographers and news organizations must avoid publishing staged or orchestrated scenes presented as spontaneous documentary events (the page uses phrasing such as “staged for the benefit of the cameras”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: allegations of press tours arranged by parties (Hezbollah) where ambulances were asked to switch on sirens and lights; accusations of people feigning death (later retracted in some cases). Journalists should be skeptical of orchestrated displays and investigate the circumstances of press access and control by interested parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism toward improbable composition (pristine items in rubble)
rubrics_metrics.description: Question photographs that show improbably undamaged or pristine items (e.g., intact photographs or photo albums sitting undisturbed on top of rubble) which may indicate staging or fabrication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CAMERA and others highlighted such suspicious recurring motifs (toys, intact photos) across multiple agencies' images; guidance is to verify provenance and chain-of-custody and ask how such objects could plausibly remain pristine in the depicted scenario.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate captioning and timestamp transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure captions accurately describe content and time; be aware of time-stamp inconsistencies introduced by news feeds/websites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page documents cases of improperly captioned images (e.g., The New York Times online edition miscaptioning an injured rescue worker) and multiple time-stamped images of the same person appearing with different agencies. Guidance: verify original agency metadata, explain feed time-stamp behavior, and issue corrections when errors are discovered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify sequence/context before alleging staging
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not draw conclusions about staging without examining the full photographic sequence and additional frames; initial single-frame readings can be misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: critique that a man was ‘pretending to be dead’ was reversed after examination of several stills showing he was in fact dead. Guidance: analyze image sequences, corroborating evidence, and eyewitness/medical reports before asserting staging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use forensic and independent investigation to adjudicate disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: Use formal forensic methods or independent investigations (e.g., Human Rights Watch forensic investigation) rather than solely relying on blog claims or conjecture to determine authenticity and cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: HRW’s forensic investigation into the Qana ambulance incident concluded there was no hoax and suggested specific munition types; the page also shows academic and expert disagreement (e.g., critique by Professor Avi Bell). Guidance: rely on documented on-site forensic analysis and transparent methodology when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vetting, accountability and oversight of freelance photographers
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations must vet and hold accountable freelance photographers whose images they publish; failures may lead to ending relationships and withdrawing images from sale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated actions: Reuters stopped cooperation with Adnan Hajj, withdrew all his photos (920 images), and an internal investigation led to dismissal of an editor. Guidance: maintain oversight of freelancers’ portfolios, check metadata, and investigate anomalies in freelancers’ work (some critics suggested checking expenses for unexplained purchases in relation to staged props).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency, correction and removal when errors are found
rubrics_metrics.description: When manipulated, miscaptioned or otherwise erroneous images are published, media organizations should be transparent, correct the record and remove or withdraw affected images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Reuters issued advisories, removed altered images, apologized and said corrected versions would follow; The New York Times issued corrections on captions. Guidance: publish clear corrections, explain the nature of the error, and remove doctored material from distribution/sales databases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution before accusing individuals or groups of propaganda using images
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercise care before publicly accusing individuals (e.g., civil defence personnel) or groups of using bodies or images for propaganda without robust evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page records accusations (e.g., Salam Daher) followed by contested evidence; guidance: corroborate with multiple sources and avoid amplifying unverified allegations that can harm reputations and mislead readers.
